summary: Offers views from MITRE and IBM authors on data sharing across the ARPANET. They support the idea of a committee to classify the issues, integrate separate data activities and coordinate experiments, as suggested by Arie Shoshani.

plainLanguage.summary: This position paper supports forming a committee to coordinate data-sharing work on the ARPA Network. It describes three possible stages of access and suggests areas to develop and test.

subtitle: A position paper proposing a committee to coordinate data-sharing work on the ARPA Network.

tldr.problem: Independent network projects addressed data handling separately, and their approaches needed coordination.
tldr.mechanism: The authors support a committee to classify issues, integrate ongoing work, and coordinate experiments across three stages of data access.
tldr.outcome: This is a discussion paper for a data-sharing meeting, not a specific implementation or protocol design.

sections.title: A Committee for Data Sharing
sections.content:
Karp, McKay and Wood support Arie Shoshani's suggestion in RFC 140 to form a committee on data sharing. They propose that the committee classify issues and possible approaches, bring independent network activities together, and coordinate experiments to test services and compare alternatives.

This paper is intended as a basis for discussion at a data-sharing meeting. It does not try to specify implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors want a committee to help separate data-sharing problems and coordinate work on possible solutions. They offer these views for a meeting discussion.

sections.title: Three Stages of Data Access
sections.content:
The authors describe three stages of data sharing. In Stage 1, a user connects directly to a host providing a data service, such as through Telnet or a known socket. In Stage 2, an intermediate data control facility routes requests, but the user still identifies the services to use.

In Stage 3, the user treats the network as a single resource and refers to data by name. A data control facility would locate the appropriate services and combine them when needed. The stages are not necessarily sequential.
sections.plainLanguage: Users could first contact each data service directly, then use a helper to route requests, and eventually ask for data by name without knowing where it is stored.

sections.title: Areas for Development
sections.content:
The paper identifies a data description language for defining physical and logical file structures and fields; a control or access language that can map to different data-management languages; and methods for managing and merging distributed data, searching directories and recovering from errors.

Existing services should fit into a coordinated design. The authors cite the Data Reconfiguration Service in RFC 138 for transformations, say file transfer should be consistent with other data services, and suggest that CCA's data machine and the network machine concept in RFC 51 could contribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee should help create shared ways to describe files, request data and handle errors. Existing tools should be able to work together.

sections.title: Experiments and Coordination
sections.content:
The authors recommend testing individual services and how they work together, as well as comparing alternative approaches. Suggested experiments include transferring files between systems, moving databases to the data computer, presenting data in a logical structure while preserving its physical structure, and automating data transformations.

They also call for experiments on consistency when duplicate files are updated and on access controls for private data. The proposed committee should coordinate development, maintain consistency among services and test them as they are implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing should cover file transfer, data conversion, consistency between copies and privacy controls. The committee would coordinate those experiments.
